fig_growth.webp.summary: The number of economic evaluations has grown rapidly. Half of the included research was published from 2020 onwards. The 2026 count covers only part of the year.

fig_method_stream.webp.title: How studies measure health benefits is changing
fig_method_stream.webp.summary: More studies now use measures that combine length and quality of life. These measures help compare health benefits across different diseases. The 2026 count is incomplete.

fig_disease_circular.webp.summary: This chart shows which disease groups receive the most research attention. A study can cover several groups, so the percentages can add up to more than 100%. Only studies with disease information are included.

fig_transition.webp.summary: Research in lower-income countries has shifted towards long-term conditions, alongside changes in disease burden.

paper04.webp.title: Disease priorities are changing in lower-income countries
paper04.webp.summary: Compare the diseases studied in earlier and later years. Infectious diseases account for a smaller share of research in lower-income settings, while cancer and respiratory disease account for more. Studies can cover several disease groups.

paper05.webp.title: The diseases studied differ by country income
paper05.webp.summary: Infectious diseases feature more often in research about lower-income countries. Cancer and heart disease feature more often in higher-income settings. A study can appear in more than one disease group.

fig_intervention_map.webp.title: What kinds of healthcare does the research cover?
fig_intervention_map.webp.summary: Each point represents a study. Nearby points have similar abstract text. The colours show the type of healthcare studied and its focus on lower-income countries; the point positions do not represent geographic locations.

fig_theme_rank.webp.title: Research topics differ between higher- and lower-income countries
fig_theme_rank.webp.summary: Compare the topics most concentrated in higher-income settings with those most concentrated in lower-income settings. These are the two ends of the topic range, rather than a list of the most commonly studied topics overall.

fig_intervention_mix.webp.title: What gets evaluated: types of healthcare by country income
fig_intervention_mix.webp.summary: Compare the share of studies evaluating medicines, vaccines, surgery and other types of healthcare. Each study is counted under its main intervention. The chart includes studies about one country with known income.

paper01.webp.title: How records were selected for the evidence map
paper01.webp.summary: The map includes 41,657 economic evaluation records, including 1,706 reviews identified from their titles. The diagram shows how records moved through screening and selection; review status has not been verified for every record.

fig_metric.webp.title: How health benefits are measured differs by country income
fig_metric.webp.summary: Studies use measures of healthy life gained or illness avoided. A QALY combines length and quality of life; a DALY measures healthy life lost to illness or early death. A study may report either, both or neither.

paper02.webp.title: Studies using models more often report measures that compare health benefits across diseases
paper02.webp.summary: Compare studies that estimate costs and outcomes with a model and studies that measure them in patients. The chart shows how often they report QALYs or DALYs, which help compare health benefits across diseases.

fig_intervention_decision.webp.title: What studies report to help healthcare decisions
fig_intervention_decision.webp.summary: Compare reporting across types of healthcare. The chart checks for information about value for money, uncertainty and whose costs are considered. It uses what is reported in abstracts, so a missing item does not mean the study did not address it.

fig_dotmap.svg.summary: Each bubble represents a country; larger bubbles mean more economic evaluations mention it. Colours show country income. A study covering several countries can appear in several bubbles.

fig_worldmap.webp.summary: This map compares the number of evaluations with each country's population. It shows research coverage rather than the quality of the evidence or the amount of funding received.

paper03.webp.title: How much research is available relative to population?
paper03.webp.summary: Compare economic evaluation counts per 10 million people across country income groups. This adjusts for population size, but does not measure research quality or whether enough evidence exists.

fig_authorship_pattern.webp.title: Are local researchers involved in studies about their countries?
fig_authorship_pattern.webp.summary: Compare studies with authors based in the country studied and studies involving authors based elsewhere. Author location is based on recorded institutional affiliations, which may be incomplete.

fig_forest.webp.title: Local authorship differs across regions
fig_forest.webp.summary: Most studies about a country include an author based there, but this happens less often in sub-Saharan Africa. Author location comes from recorded affiliations and does not establish who led the study.

paper06.webp.title: Some studies about lower-income countries have no locally based author
paper06.webp.summary: Nearly a third of studies about low-income countries have no author with a recorded affiliation there. Missing or incomplete affiliations can affect this estimate; local authorship does not necessarily mean local leadership.

fig_collab_chord.webp.title: How researchers collaborate across country income groups
fig_collab_chord.webp.summary: The connections show collaboration between authors based in different income groups. Higher-income teams form a central part of the network. Recorded affiliations identify author locations, rather than funding or study leadership.

fig_research_burden_ratio.svg.summary: Each point is a country's share of economic evaluations divided by its share of disease burden. Points below the proportional line have less research than their share of burden; the bar in each income group marks the median. The typical low-income country has about 10 times less research than its burden share, while the typical high-income country has about twice as much. Hollow points rest on fewer than five studies. Proportional is a reference point, not a target for how much research a country should receive.

paper07.webp.summary: Compare how many economic evaluations countries have relative to illness and early death. The comparison adjusts for disease burden, but does not determine how much research a country needs.

fig_burden_disease_companion.webp.title: Does research attention match the burden of different diseases?
fig_burden_disease_companion.webp.summary: Compare each disease group's share of research with its share of illness and early death. This helps identify areas receiving relatively less research attention; it is not a recommended funding allocation.

paper08.webp.title: Some disease groups receive less research attention relative to their burden
paper08.webp.summary: Injuries, and mental health and substance use in poorer settings, show particularly large differences between research attention and disease burden. The comparison is a reference point rather than a funding target.

fig_deficit.webp.title: Where are the largest differences between research and disease burden?
fig_deficit.webp.summary: This chart highlights the largest differences between research output and disease burden. It does not estimate the cost of filling an evidence gap or prove that a particular funding allocation would be best.

fig_injustice.webp.title: How research attention compares with disease burden worldwide
fig_injustice.webp.summary: Compare where research is concentrated with where illness and early death occur. Equal shares provide a reference for comparison, rather than a target for research or funding.

fig_inequality.webp.title: How research coverage varies with disease burden
fig_inequality.webp.summary: Compare the amount of research available with the level of illness and early death. A low study count does not by itself show whether the evidence is sufficient or useful.

fig_openaccess.webp.summary: More economic evaluations are available to read without paying. The chart uses recorded open-access status; unknown access status is not treated as paywalled.

fig_funder_funders.svg.title: Top donors: who funds economic evaluations, and where?
fig_funder_funders.svg.summary: The bars show how many studies report each funder, rather than how much money they provided. Only about 27% of studies report a funder in the dataset, so this is an incomplete picture. Colours show study setting; grey retains other settings and missing income information.

fig_map_burden.webp.title: Where is research more or less abundant relative to disease burden?
fig_map_burden.webp.summary: This map compares research coverage with illness and early death. It shows relative research attention, rather than whether a country has enough evidence or should receive a particular funding amount.

fig_map_openaccess.webp.title: Where is evidence available to read for free?
fig_map_openaccess.webp.summary: Compare recorded open-access availability across countries. Access information is incomplete; an unknown status does not necessarily mean an article requires payment.

fig_map_growth.webp.summary: Compare how economic evaluation output has grown across countries. Growth describes publication counts rather than evidence quality. The final publication year is incomplete.

fig_map_authorship.webp.title: Where do studies include locally based authors?
fig_map_authorship.webp.summary: This map shows whether studies include an author based in the country studied. It uses recorded affiliations, which can be incomplete, and does not establish who led the research.

fig_map_model.webp.title: Where do studies estimate outcomes with models or measure them in patients?
fig_map_model.webp.summary: Compare studies using models to estimate costs and health outcomes with those drawing on measured patient outcomes. This describes their approach, rather than judging their quality.

fig_equity_time.webp.title: A growing share of research focuses on lower-income countries
fig_equity_time.webp.summary: Track the share of economic evaluations about low- and middle-income countries over time. Publication counts show research attention, rather than funding amounts or evidence quality.

fig_reach_time.webp.title: More countries now have at least one economic evaluation
fig_reach_time.webp.summary: Track how many countries are mentioned in at least one included evaluation. Having one study indicates some coverage; it does not mean there is enough evidence for all healthcare decisions.

fig_decision_time.webp.title: Studies increasingly report information that helps assess value for money
fig_decision_time.webp.summary: Track how often abstracts mention costs relative to health benefits, uncertainty and other information useful for decisions. These are abstract-based checks; an item may be addressed in the full paper even if it is absent from the abstract.

fig_funder_opportunity.webp.title: Where is research least abundant relative to health needs?
fig_funder_opportunity.webp.summary: Explore areas with relatively little evidence compared with disease burden. These comparisons help identify questions for further investigation; they do not estimate the cost or benefit of funding new research.

fig_funder_scorecard.webp.title: Compare evidence gaps that funders could investigate
fig_funder_scorecard.webp.summary: Compare indicators of research coverage and health needs. The ranking is a starting point for discussion, rather than a funding recommendation or an estimate of value for money.

fig_funder_capacity.webp.title: Where could local research capacity be strengthened?
fig_funder_capacity.webp.summary: Compare indicators of local research participation and evidence coverage. These signals can guide further investigation, but do not directly measure skills, infrastructure or the cost of building research capacity.

fig_funder_trajectory.webp.title: Which evidence gaps are narrowing over time?
fig_funder_trajectory.webp.summary: Compare changes in research coverage over time. Past publication trends show what has happened, rather than predicting future research or funding needs.

fig_wellcome_priorities.svg.title: Wellcome-funded studies across the priority themes
fig_wellcome_priorities.svg.summary: This chart counts studies that report Wellcome Trust as a funder in each theme, with Wellcome's share of theme studies and its rank among reported funders. The grey bar shows studies outside all three themes. Disease groups provide broad theme indicators, and Climate & Health uses a provisional title screen. Themes can overlap; these counts are not a complete record of Wellcome grants.

wellcome_analysis.html.summary: Explore the evidence and recorded funders within Wellcome's priority themes. The view separates all theme-related studies from Wellcome-funded studies. Theme coverage and funding records are incomplete; Climate & Health classification is provisional.

fig_glance_regions.html.title: Research coverage and health needs by region
fig_glance_regions.html.summary: Compare regions' research coverage, disease focus and health needs. Use the information buttons to see how each measure was calculated. These comparisons describe evidence coverage, rather than recommending a funding allocation.
